newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil seen leaving rates steady on U.S. Fed move.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seen leaving rates steady on U.S. Fed move.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to leave U.S. interest rates unchanged reinforces most market expectations that Brazil will hold monthly rates steady when policy-makers meet Wednesday, analysts said.
Brazil's Monetary Policy Committee (COPOM) is due to meet to set the Central Bank's Basic Interest Rate, or TBC, and the Basic Assistance Rate, known as TBAN, for June.

Analysts expect the TBC and TBAN rates to remain unchanged from May's 1.58 percent and 1.78 percent, respectively, as steady U.S. rates have eliminated fears the government would be forced to raise domestic rates to lure foreign capital.

"If the Fed decided to raise rates, (the Central Bank) would have two options: increase domestic rates or leave them unchanged. Now it can work with steady rates or even a slight cut," said Jose Mauro Delella, economist at Lloyds Bank, Brazil.
Higher U.S. rates would encourage foreigners to reduce investments abroad, particularly in emerging markets.
Despite the possibility of a slight reduction, most analysts bet the government will continue to use high interest rates to have better control of its external accounts.
Brazil's projected $35-36 billion current account gap this year is the main reason for the government to be conservative in terms of monetary policy, they said.
Lower foreign reserves also helped increasing market concerns. In the last four months, Brazil lost nearly $4.0 billion in reserves, which are now at $56 billion.

"By maintaining the rates unchanged, the government would show it is concerned and is moving to have better control of its foreign accounts," said Andre Carvalho, economist at Banco Fonte Cindam. But Carvalho sees room for gradual and slight declines in the second half of the year.
Brazil's Central Bank suspended its policy of gradually lowering interest rates in May, when it left the TBC rate unchanged from April.
The Fed's move to leave U.S. rates at the same levels were also seen as positive for Brazil's stock market, analysts said.
Higher rates would be an additional factor unsettling the markets, already unstable by an alleged cash-for-votes scandal involving a re-election bill, they said.
"Higher rates would intensify nervousness in the markets," said Lloyd's Delella.
Local share prices erased early losses and ended higher Tuesday after the Fed's decision was announced.
